One night, on her way back from the library, Frostia looked up at the stars, and suddenly realized that the paths they drew matched the ones in her mind. Her gaze wandered through the sky just as her fingers once wandered through the pages of a book.

She began to linger beneath the stars.
In the courtyard garden, under the veil of night,
her small figure stood on tiptoe each evening, peering into a telescope. The faint glow on her tails flickered in harmony with the starlight above.
But soon, amidst the scattered starlight, shooting stars began falling at her feet, and no one knew why...

The scholars at the Academia temporarily banned her from stargazing, but the unexplainable "mysteries" didn't stop.
Faint footsteps echoed through grand, empty hallways; neatly arranged books on shelves would suddenly collapse into disarray...

The rumors and mysterious happenings hadn't gone unnoticed. But before the scholars could ask, Frostia appeared at their office on her own.

"Professor... could my stargazing dreams be prophetic?" She recounted the dream she'd had the night before: an unexpected impact somewhere, countless shards of light raining down on crowds...
The professor extended his hand to her. "If you want to find out, you'll have to step beyond the library."

Before her lay a path she had never taken.
Behind her, the terrifying visions from her dream still lingered in her mind.

For the sake of people she had never met, she boarded a train for the very first time, and set off into the vast unknown.

So she turned around and peered carefully, checking left and right. After a moment of searching, she finally spotted Nanda flailing and gesturing wildly at her.
Seeing that Iara had finally noticed him, Nanda let out a happy sigh of relief. Thank goodness he caught her before she opened the little paper ball.

"For... who?" Iara mouthed, tilting her head while the teacher wasn't looking. Nanda pointed at the seat next to her, winking and pulling exaggerated faces in the same direction, terrified she'd get it wrong.

Iara gave him a small nod. The next time the teacher turned around, she successfully slipped the note to its destination. Before sitting back up straight, she caught Nanda giving her a big thumbs-up out of the corner of her eye.

Joining in on this kind of wild group activity once in a while wasn't so bad, Iara thought.

Next was activity class, and almost everyone headed out to the field.
Not wanting to test the "wherever Iara goes, it rains" rule again, she went to the reading room as usual.

She sat by the window and flipped through book after book, but she just couldn't focus. After reading only a few lines of each, her gaze would drift back out the window toward the field.
She sat there distracted for a good while before finally sighing and deciding to put the books back on the shelf.
When she returned to the window after putting everything away, she realized the sun was already setting. And everyone on the field... was gone?

Was school over? She hadn't heard the bell... Iara was still trying to figure it out when the reading room doors suddenly burst open. Nanda rushed in like a gust of wind, grabbed her hand, and started running. "Iara, let's go! I'll take you to see the sun!"

Nanda pulled Iara through the light drizzle until they reached a large tree in the corner of the field. It turned out everyone was gathered right here.

"Lights! Lights!" Nanda shouted. Someone in the crowd flipped a switch, and the tree lit up.
It was only then that Iara noticed all sorts of "suns" hanging from the branches in different shapes and sizes. Not only did they glow, but they even had hand-cranked gears to make them rise and set.

Wait, drop that right now! Strange, this was supposed to be a journey that took them farther and farther away from home, but with Doggie's company, every day, he felt blessed with luck like all the days before. Still, danger and uncertainty drew ever closer, and when he picked up the dull cracking sounds echoing through the quiet mountains, he knew an avalanche was coming. By the time he woke up between a slush of mud and snow, he had no idea how long he'd been buried. A wet tongue licked his eyes, blurring the moon in his vision, and under it, he saw Doggie whimpering and digging through the snow. So the deity has blessed me after all! he thought and smiled, not daring to make a sound for fear of stirring the mountain again. Doggie had suffered a broken hind leg and a gash on its scalp. Dorjelang applied some medicinal herbs to the wound and grabbed some foxtail to weave a little hat, so as to keep Doggie from scratching its head. Holding his companion, Dorjelang thought about turning back to their village, but the way back was even longer than continuing forward. Doggie barked furiously in protest, as if to say, "All my work would have been for nothing if you turned back now." Man and dog then traveled even farther.

Orange like the sun, yet not as vast or as daunting. She thought with relief that maybe the stars, of all things, were just the right warmth. "Those are human torches." Her companion said and turned away. The soft hem of their garment swayed in the water, and the waves in the wake of their departure bobbed Nerina up and down. Even so, she kept her gaze upward, watching as the "starlight" drifted closer, then slowly away again. "Tor... ches." The word lingered in Nerina's mind like a melody, yet she couldn't form its shape. What are torches? And what do they sound like...? Her companion had already left the grove, leaving only a trail of bubbles behind. The bubbles carried a message, urging her on: "Hurry. You'll be late for class." It's not my fault that composition is so boring. Nerina plucked at the lyre strings while spacing out. Nobody really wanted to be there for the dull lesson. A coral pointer struck her lyre, breaking her out of her reverie. Seeing the teacher about to puff up like a frustrated balloon, Nerina quickly raised her hand to rejoin the orchestra's melody — a tedious, solemn, and weighty piece as slow as a sea turtle. All raised hands in the classroom then descended onto the strings in gentle, graceful arcs. Sometimes pausing for a second, other times much longer, long enough for a tiny planula to mature into a massive coral. Only after such an agonizingly long wait would the next note of the section slowly emerge. This was the same section where Nerina almost passed out from holding her breath during the previous rehearsal. And when the next note finally came, she nearly drowned herself again with deep, desperate inhales. She refused to move her hand again, because she couldn't fathom the meaning behind the piece. Maybe it was about an old sea turtle taking a stroll, or even the lives of seahorses, who were often motionless between the corals. In any case, it certainly wasn't a hymn that praised and celebrated the gift of joy from the Ocean God, as her teacher had claimed.

And yet, Mo Ji soon began a strange kind of "communication" between them.
Whenever Harpeno deliberately went against the navigator's instructions, venting a frustration she couldn't quite name, a new map would appear in her locker the next day. Every wrong turn was marked in red, with a small stick figure doodled beside it, fuming with anger. She would scribble "Mind your own business" across the page. In reply, Mo Ji would sketch a girl covering her ears in the corner, neatly labeled: "Signal reception weak."

Gradually, Harpeno came to realize that Mo Ji's maps were more than routes. They were a language of their own. Color intensity indicated the severity of obstacles. Line weight marked their size. Vivid, concrete depictions made it easy to see what would otherwise be hard to picture. This was not something taught in textbooks. It was a private code, entirely her own.

The turning point came during the feared stardust belt navigation exam before graduation.
As Harpeno approached the target zone, the navigator began to glitch, and every instrument flickered wildly. Amidst the chaos at the exam control center, Mo Ji burst in, took the communicator, and made herself heard for the first time in three years—
"Trust your eyes, Harpeno!" Her voice was hoarse but steady. "Half a turn right. That nebula ahead isn't real. It's a debris field! Trust me. You can see it."
Harpeno held her breath. Her gaze pierced through the interference, and sure enough, there was a hidden safe passage. Mo Ji had already mapped the area in greater detail than any navigation system could. And in that moment, she chose to trust Harpeno's eyes over every instrument.

On the 364th day of his fourteenth year, Msafiri became a "runaway" on the eve of his adulthood.

He still remembered that phone call from Driftingale Guild years ago, which wasn't meant for him, but still...
It quietly planted the seed of a dream that hot summer afternoon, one of measuring every planet and every islet with his own eyes, ears, and feet. And where better to start than the very place that he called home?

Msafiri chose the perfect day to set out, with the intention of making this his very own special coming-of-age gift.
However, trials were afoot for these nascent dreams and their dreamer. And just like that, Msafiri lost his way.
The lack of experience and days of roughing it in the wilderness had taught Msafiri harsh lessons. He'd never felt this challenged back when he hunted with his parents and little brother. Only now did he realize that he wasn't quite the skilled hunter he thought himself to be out here on the plains, let alone finding directions, plotting routes, or setting up camp... All that condensed theory and knowledge in textbooks proved painfully shallow when the time came for him to apply them.

Fleeing the southern winter, the young man cradled the sprig of red plum blossoms to his chest, carefully guarding it against the rocking of the boat that bore him toward home. 

To little Heyu, the journey felt agonizingly long. So long that the moment he closed his eyes, Sister Jiu would appear. He would see her leaning against the window, quietly unraveling the faded characters of an ancient book. And every time, he found himself burning to ask her: Why must our people live in hiding? Why is the road home so endlessly, unfathomably long?

"To keep from being found, of course." The memory, hazy and yellowed with time, suddenly found its voice. He realized with a pang that he had almost forgotten how she sounded. "That place... only those drawn by fate will ever find it. And when that moment comes, you will feel it, too."

I used to live on Gem Street. Every day, I'd get woken up at the exact same time, climb up to the roof, and watch the bustling tourists flood the Planette. Then I'd expose the shady gem merchants, get into an argument, and finally "reason" with them by smashing a nearby chunk of ore with a single smack.

At night, I'd crouch on the roof. Thanks to my shiny, reflective eyes, people would mistake me for the legendary glowing lanterns of the Gem Night Market.

I got chased by the blacksmith because I couldn't stop drooling while watching the ore forging process. In a panic, I scrambled onto a departing travel cart... well, the roof of it, anyway.

I found myself in an unfamiliar place. I was totally bewildered, but quickly regained my composure, sat right down, and started to think.
The conclusion I came to was that I absolutely had to have stew for lunch today.
And somehow, my journey to find rare ores and stew began...

Together, the two of them sang the song once more. Their voices and the lyre's melody made ripples through time, travelling from the island of yesteryear to the boat in the present before finally landing warmly back onto the sea. Rebella soon realized that her master's humble gemstone workshop was the quietest place on the entire street. She sat on the rooftop, letting the wind pass her by, but couldn't figure it out. In the end, she hopped down.
"Master, what does family even mean?" Rebella asked.

The craftsman lifted his gaze from the polishing wheel and looked at Rebella, now seated beside him.
"Family, sweethearts, friends... all of them are essentially just labels and categories," he said. "Fragile, yet enduring. Sometimes, those labels give us a sense of security. But what truly matters is where you are, and what it is you really want."

Rebella seemed to catch hold of something unseen. "Then what do you want most?"
The man looked up toward a gap in the roof, where a strip of sky showed through.
"You know... there is a tri-colored gemstone mentioned in the old records, one that can bathe the land in dazzling hues at sunrise."
Wiping the sweat from his brow, her master spoke of a dream of a tri-colored gemstone.

Although the dream had nothing to do with Rebella, it piqued her curiosity nonetheless. From that day on, she began traveling with him, climbing mountains and crossing rivers in search of stones with strange and wondrous colors.

Magic Wheel Rules:
1. Use a Hat-Trick Magic Ticket and guess a number on the wheel to participate in the Hat-Trick Magic Wheel.
2. After the first participant begins the Hat-Trick Magic Wheel, a 30-second participation period will begin. During this time, all joining players will participate in the same round.
3. The results are announced after the spin. If any participant in the round wins a Gold Prize, all other participants will receive a bonus reward.
4. There is a daily limit to how many bonus rewards each player can receive. Once this limit is reached, no further bonus rewards will be granted.

Prize Rules:
1. Before spinning the wheel, choose a number from 1 to 6.
2. Once the wheel stops, if your chosen number matches the result, you win the Gold Prize. If your number is exactly 2 away from the result, you win the Silver Prize. All other numbers win the Bronze Prize.
3. Before each spin, you can choose how many Hat-Trick Magic Tickets to use. Each ticket grants 1 prize, and you can use up to 5 tickets per spin.

Prize Distribution:
1. After the results are announced, head to the prize pile next to Civilla to claim your reward bundle(s).
2. Once you have claimed your reward bundle(s), you can join the next round of the wheel.
3. Civilla will regularly update the items in the bundles, so stay tuned!

Duplicate Prizes:

1. Prizes that can be obtained multiple times will be issued as normal.
2. Prizes that cannot be obtained multiple times will automatically convert into other rewards. Please refer to the actual items received.

It was an evening ten years ago. "One, two, three..." "One, two, three, four, five..." Young Msafiri, who had just learned to count, was squatting on the ground and enthusiastically tracing the geometric patterns his mother had drawn around their camp. Three points, in groups of five — he shared the pattern he discovered with his little brother, who was still too young to speak. His brother tilted his head and twitched his ears, listening intently even if he didn't understand a word. The tantalizing smell of roasted meat from the campfire teased young Msafiri's nose, and his empty stomach growled shamelessly in protest. Nope, no food until I learn this! he silently vowed. ... Msafiri twitched his ears and wrinkled his nose as the memories came. The wild winds indiscriminately assaulted all in its path, chilling travelers to the bone. It had been three days and three nights, and Msafiri still hadn't tracked down any prey. The memories of roasted meat could no longer make him salivate. Forget about exploring the planet under these conditions — it was much more likely for him to end up a desiccated corpse and become one with this wilderness. Msafiri could draw beautiful and elegant geometric patterns by hand now, but the question of his survival hung by a thread. Could those patterns truly evoke ancient protection...? Msafiri wondered as he found a branch that could barely support his rest. He stared into the seemingly unchanging starry night and recalled another memory.

The flowers here... could talk? She pushed herself to her feet and brushed the dirt from her dress. Thankfully, her coiffure was still intact. As her gaze wandered, she realized it wasn't just the flowers. Everything in the garden seemed to be watching her: a tiny clay pot, a single blade of grass, a little trowel, a clump of mud, even a patch of soil! They all stared with wide, curious eyes and wore friendly, if a little odd, expressions. They were far from perfect. Far from refined. Each of them was rough and earthy in its own way. And yet, Medowlyn felt a strange, familiar warmth. With a startled shriek, she turned and ran down the path.

The repairman patching a bike tire called it out to the passing peddler— "The Yuns' kid is missing!" Did it matter whether anyone actually knew who the Yuns were? Not a bit. Just spread the word. Nothing could go wrong if everyone helped look. Blushberry — that was the kid who never smiled, the one who burst into tears the moment she saw a stranger. Granny was by the well in front of the bamboo house, washing mugwort leaves when she caught wind of it. She always boiled them in summer for the little one's bath, to keep the mosquitoes away and keep the rash at bay... Wait, who did you say was missin'? "Told you, her Gramps's no good at mindin' kids." Grabbing her palm fan, she charged down the mountain. The search party for Blushberry stirred the entire mountain. By the time the sun was about to set, everyone finally let out a breath of relief.

The first among them to think of leaving was his buddy. Pulling Dorjelang along, he made grand plans of how he would conquer the endless mountains and see the world beyond in pursuit of his dreams. Dreams? What are... dreams? Buddies stick together till the end, so you're coming too, Dorjelang. Dorjelang was worried that he'd hold his buddy back, being as frail as he was. But his friend had unwavering faith in him. Before they left, his buddy got caught "loaning" a couple of barley buns from an old herder. Dorjelang went for the rescue, but froze at the doorway. "HAHMM? You have no right to keep him on the pastures forever..." On the glimmering highlands where heaven is just a few steps away, too many struggle to make the journey because of a weighted heart. "You've never believed in him. You just think he's weak, and needs protection..." Outside the house, Dorjelang listened as Doggie came over. As always, it sat beside him, panting with a lolling tongue, as if saying, "Eavesdropping too, huh?" "How long will you deceive him with these words? Are you going to keep sheltering him his whole life?" Dorjelang gazed up at the sunset's glow, at the deity watching over the highlands. "There is no divine blessing. He has the same horns and fur on his head as us, plus a yak horn hat that I traded with barley buns..." Please let all my good fortune rest upon my buddy's head— "I have my own dreams and my own path to follow, so I won't stay... but save half the barley bun for him. I'm leaving this place..." May he be safe, free, and prosperous on the journey of his dreams. This was Dorjelang's sixteenth year living on the highland pastures. In the empty house his buddy left behind, the old herder threw him a bundle of supplies, his mustache bristling with anger. He told Dorjelang to get out there and bring back his good-for-nothing buddy. Finally, he understood there was a kind of longing in this world that words cannot capture. He wanted to cross this mountain, and the next one beyond, and countless more after.

Maybe it was his loud hisses, or maybe it was the hypnotic dance of the campfire... either way, Msafiri couldn't remember what exactly happened after. He vaguely recalled his mother telling him a story while pointing at the stars in the sky. A story about those geometric patterns. Perhaps it was time to visit home after this expedition? It had been long since he last went back. But for now, Msafiri felt his eyelids grow heavy and allowed the night to gently shut his eyes. Just a brief nap... a micro-nap that won't do any harm, he comforted himself. Frost began to form on top of his lashes as they quivered in the wind, but the bonfire in his dreams was simply so warm that he didn't want to wake up. "Once upon a time..." It was choir practice day.
As usual, Iara stood right in the center, surrounded by everyone.
She didn't actually think she was a great singer, but the spot had seemingly defaulted to her since day one.

On that first day, she had stood on stage to introduce herself. Barely a second after she said her name, someone in the crowd cheered.
"Wow! What a pretty name! It's like a mermaid!"
"She must be great at singing!"
"Awesome, we've got a lead singer!"
Others whispered among themselves, "Isn't her mom that famous singer..."
And so, it just sort of happened. Nobody ever asked Iara if she actually wanted to do it.

As the all-too-familiar warm-up song began, Iara let her mind wander while she sang...

What did she want to be when she grew up?
It was a question Iara had never really thought about before. She'd never had the time to.
Her schedule was packed tight for at least three hundred days a year. Mama Xida, who took care of Iara, always joked that their little Iara was almost busier than the president of Loomix Co.

Iara had never met the president of Loomix Co., but she'd heard the merchants at the market mention him. They said he was a very important and clever businessman, so of course someone like that would be incredibly busy.
Hmm... Business? She didn't think she had any talent for that.
What about other jobs, then? What would she end up doing? Suddenly, Iara felt a little excited about growing up.
...

The melody grew more intense, shifting into an imposing shade of red. Iara didn't like it.
She quietly lowered her voice until she was just mouthing the words, her eyes fixed on the rain outside the window as she continued to daydream.

It was Dorjelang's first day at the Galactic Bazaar. All his life, he had felt adrift in a vast sea of people — without direction, without a place to belong. After hauling five boxes of goods for a shopkeeper at the street corner, it suddenly occurred to him that everyone here was so small, and he was incredibly strong in comparison... Maybe... I can actually help them? The revelation filled him with unprecedented joy and the urge to act, but he must stay calm. A slight turn of his body was enough to send someone flying... Mmmooo? Wasn't someone here just now? After eight victims, six cracked chairs, four shattered steps, and three flattened billboards, all eyes were trained on him with terror. He spent all his money making amends, then hurried through every intersection, anxiously avoiding anyone who came too close. Finally, he found a quiet corner to settle in. Crouching down, he took a deep breath and reminded himself to exercise more self-restraint. When he lifted his head again, he realized he was at a high point in the bazaar. Following the sound of music, he saw cheerful crowds, lively stages, and a shimmering magician's tent below...

This was Harpeno's first time handling rush hour on her own. Three cargo trucks created a complete gridlock at the intersection while fighting for the right of way, and a long line of angry, honking vehicles stretched behind them. A few drivers leaned against their doors, pontificating about the day's big Starsea news, and couldn't care less when they saw Harpeno's patrol car approaching.

"Little lady, get your supervisor," a stubbly-faced truck driver waved dismissively at her. "This isn't the place to play house."
Harpeno was silent. Her boot heels clicked against the pavement as she walked straight between the three deadlocked trucks.
"First truck." She pointed at the stubbly-faced driver's vehicle. "Your transport permit expired three months ago."
She turned to the next two trucks and continued, "Second truck, you're overloaded. Third truck, your right rear brake light is out."
She swiftly wrote out three tickets to follow.
"Now," she looked up. "Do I need to teach you gentlemen how to reverse, too?"
The three drivers' expressions immediately changed.
"Do you have any idea what we're hauling? You think you can afford to pay for the delay?"
"I certainly can't, but I can make you pay a whole lot more." She waved her ticket book. "Want to try me?"

"Nobles who obtained the seed sought to prove their power and prestige. Artists who found it wished to display their refinement and taste. Wealthy merchants who got their hands on it longed to flaunt their riches before the world.
Each planted it with care, treating it like gold, yet none waited long enough to see it sprout. Tired of waiting, they called it filthy and foul, ugly and useless, and cast it aside.
Then a farmer found the seed. To him, it was simply a seed, planted alongside his other crops. Before long, it sprouted and bloomed, bright red like the sun.
The farmer went about his daily work in the fields, pausing now and then to admire its petals and leaves, offering a smile as he carried away its scent. That fragrance, once it brushed against anyone who came near, would linger with them forever."

They continued to stare at each other in confusion. Yunguo tilted her head and blinked.
"Granny... I don't quite understand."

Granny stood up, brushed the dirt from her clothes, then helped the bewildered Yunguo to her feet and patted the soil from her skirt.
"My little Blushberry," she said, "you're that seed, growing slowly, soaking up the scent of earth and grass, waiting for your day to bloom."

Yunguo's fuzzy ears twitched, and a glimmer of hope sparked in her eyes.
Granny let out a quiet sigh of relief, thinking the child had finally come around...

The other children burst into laughter, pointing at the dirt smudged through her hair. The girl looked a little embarrassed. She mumbled, as if to explain, "Miss, I just thought that flower I passed earlier... kind of looked like it was smiling!" "Flowers don't smile," the teacher said with a frown. "That shape doesn't follow the standard pattern or proportions." "But that's okay, Miss!" The girl pulled the same playful face as her flowerpot. "It doesn't have to be perfect!" "What I really made is..." "a moment of happiness turned into something that lasts!" Outside the window, Medowlyn found herself speaking the words at the very same time. So that was it. The little girl, and the garden, were both pieces of who she used to be. And that was it. It didn't have to be perfect, as long as the memory was a happy one.

Dorjelang had once been small and fragile, the kind who stayed tucked behind others, always in need of protection. But everyone in the workshop had seen him, without meaning to, snap table legs, crush teacups, and crack plates... so they could only assume the gentle giant had been far too modest about his strength. To Dorjelang, being able to use that strength to help those weaker than himself was a kind of luck he held dear. It had nothing to do with meeting anyone's expectations. It simply meant that when he wanted to help, he could. Master Mufflin, however, insisted he had yet to understand. She watched him as he left and remembered how her bright-eyed student dug her out of a pile of magazines in the basement five years ago... No, scratch that part. She had been standing atop that very pile, arms folded, quizzing him on hats, while he answered every question with ease. Learning on his own, in secret? How dare he?! In her irritation, she leapt down and twisted her ankle... No, scratch that part too. By the magazine pile, Dorjelang had been weaving with reeds, recreating every hat on those pages. The audacity to learn in secret... She turned away with a scowl. Even so, Dorjelang had earned approval with a "Be here at eight tomorrow morning." For him, it brought a different kind of joy and anticipation, something he didn't feel when helping others. Five years had passed since Dorjelang became a hat-making apprentice. On this day, he chose a dandelion to adorn the hat meant to welcome spring. With his new kit slung over his back, he set out once more. He still dreamed of the past — of jagged mountain paths strewn with stone, of snow and forests, of winds that never ceased, and of foxtail grass swaying gently in their wake. The dandelion lifted in the breeze and drifted toward distant mountains, as if gathering those dreams. He wondered who it would stir awake this time.

Before she was even as tall as a desk, she already knew her way around the vast library.
The scholars at the academy were strict, but never with her. Their voices always softened around her, even when she climbed to the tallest shelves, and even when the priceless tomes came tumbling down around her.
Everything she knew about the universe came from the library, and the library alone.
Sunlight streamed in through the towering window. While children played in the garden outside, she remained immersed in her own world, her eyes fixed on a star map in an atlas. Her tiny finger traced one star to the next, as if the universe lived at her fingertips.

"Why don't you ever go outside?" An unfamiliar child stood beside her stacks of books, head tilted in curiosity.
She looked at him, puzzled, as if the question itself made no sense.
"There's so much out there, so many things to see, to do, to discover..." The boy tried to name a thousand reasons.
She gazed through the towering window at the dust motes dancing in the slanting sunlight.
"It has everything — everything but an end."

In biology, the incredible similarity in appearance and habits between the invertebrate Hummingbird Hawkmoth and the vertebrate hummingbird is called "convergent evolution." It's generally believed that, given highly similar environments, different species will evolve with the same functional traits and gradually "converge." At the same time, because these convergent creatures occupy similar ecological niches, they generally do not co-occur.
In other words, where there are Hummingbird Hawkmoths, it's unlikely that you'll see any hummingbirds.

Seasons passed, and Tika grew a little older.
She even achieved her dream and became... half a fruit farmer.

"I'm off to the orchard!"
Tika slung on her little backpack, stuffed with her small shovel and rake, and headed out. Lately, a bunch of agriculture students had been attending workshops at the orchard. Tika always tagged along, even if she hardly understood anything they said.
But planting trees? That she definitely knew how to do. You just dig a hole, place the sapling inside, and cover it with dirt again. She had even learned a new trick recently: you have to dig the hole a little deeper for trees.
"We work with fruit trees every single day in our major," one of the senior students told Tika while breaking up the soil with a rake. She was amazed by how much passion the little kid had for fruit trees. "If you want to plant fruit trees and don't mind the hard work, you should come study agriculture with us."
But who would ever think hanging out with fruit trees was hard work? Tika stood at the far end of the student group and puffed her chest out with pride.

It was okay if she didn't become a fruit farmer right away, because from that day forward, agriculture student Tika would grow every single one of those wondrous fruits from her dreams!

It was the ninth day of Dorjelang's arduous journey across the endless mountains.
He had prepared himself for the inevitable solitude that came with leaving home, but as he woke from a dream, he found a figure basking under the moon.

Doggie, his childhood companion, had secretly followed him. He was grinning and lolling his tongue, as if to say, "Took you long enough to notice me."

The old herders used to tell the story of how a flood once swept little Dorjelang out of the shed where he'd been sunbathing. When they finally found him, Doggie was whimpering, and Dorjelang was crying even louder.

"Worthless!" She slammed the electronic navigator onto the bench in frustration. "Did they design the path with their eyes closed?!"

A folded piece of paper slid to her feet. On it was a hand-drawn campus map, with each path marked by unique visual landmarks. "Turn left at the rusted car shell," "go straight past the café with the pigeon cage," and "turn right at the yellow-hatted scarecrow." The directions were precise, but peculiar.

She looked up and saw Mo Ji, the campus "weirdo" rumored to have not spoken a word in three years.
Mo Ji stared silently at her with eyes as calm as deep space.

Day 193 since leaving Granny's place. Yunguo sat by the riverbank, her chin resting in her hands. She thought about the last packet of seeds she had planted. They should be blooming by now. Maybe there would be fruit soon... It was a shame she wouldn't get to see it. The Islet where she had planted those seeds was nowhere to be found. People always leave. She vaguely understood that. Yunguo let out a long sigh and counted the Dough and produce in her bag, trying to stay hopeful. If she didn't eat or drink, she could last another five days. Still... it was so cold. She hugged her knees and buried her face in her arms, rubbing her eyes. Suddenly, everything went dark. But she felt warm, as if she were buried in soft soil. It almost felt nice, like she could just fall asleep like that. Then she heard the wind. She heard water flowing. She heard insects chirping. She saw an earthworm wriggling beside her, loosening the soil... Wait, where did that earthworm come from?!
Sleep well.
